summary: This unit teaches you to manage the quality of guest service in a hotel, villa company or resort. You will learn the dimensions of service quality, how to set and roll out service standards, how to gather and analyse feedback and complaints with simple tools, how to recover from service failures and empower staff, how to measure and report quality, and how to build a service culture, including for guests with different needs.

blocks.p: Guests judge a hotel by how they are treated as much as by the room and the food. **Quality guest service** means consistently meeting, and where possible exceeding, what guests reasonably expect. A manager cannot be at every guest contact, so quality must be **designed** (standards), **taught** (training and coaching), **measured** (feedback and indicators) and **improved** (analysis and action).

This unit is for supervisors and managers in Jamaican hotels, villas, guest houses and resorts, where guests come from Jamaica and from abroad and many choose the destination partly on reviews. Jamaica's tourism standards are supported by the Tourism Product Development Company (TPDCo), whose Team Jamaica programme is one example of a national approach to service.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in practice
rows: Use the five dimensions of service quality, the idea of expectations and the guest experience.
Write clear, measurable service standards, procedures and a service charter; train and coach staff.
Use surveys, comment cards, online reviews, mystery guests, complaint logs and briefings.
Record complaints, calculate rates, use Pareto charts, fishbone diagrams and the five whys.
Apologise, fix, compensate fairly and follow up; empower staff with limits and controls.
Track indicators, benchmark, report to owners and evaluate improvements.
Meet diverse needs and legal duties
Serve guests with different needs; handle guest data, advertising and safety incidents properly.
Hire, brief, recognise and model good service; manage partners and plan for peak demand.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with hotel scenarios and short calculations (complaint rates, percentages, shares, value of lost guests).
A **written paper**: short answers (terms such as service recovery, Pareto chart, empowerment, mystery guest, SERVQUAL, SOP) and longer answers.
**Group practical tasks**: analysing a complaint log and presenting a service improvement plan, and role-playing service recovery and writing an empowerment guideline.

blocks.note: Work every percentage and rate twice. Most calculation marks in this unit are lost by dividing the wrong way round or by forgetting to scale to 1,000 room nights.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Guests compare what they **expect** with what they **experience**. If the experience meets or beats the expectation, they are satisfied. Expectations come from past stays, advertising, reviews, price and what staff promise. A manager must therefore manage **both** the service and the promises.

blocks.h: The five dimensions of service quality (SERVQUAL)

head: Dimension
Meaning
Hotel example
rows: The look of rooms, facilities, staff and materials
Clean rooms, working air conditioning, neat uniforms
Doing what was promised, accurately and on time
Room ready at the promised time; correct bill
Willingness to help and speed of response
Phone answered quickly; requests dealt with promptly
Knowledge, courtesy and the ability to inspire trust
Staff who know the answers and treat guests politely
Remembering a guest's preferences; noticing a guest in difficulty

blocks.p: A hotel whose rooms are rated highly but where guests wait too long for the telephone to be answered is weakest on **responsiveness**. Use the dimensions to diagnose where quality falls short.

Service quality fails when there is a **gap**. Common gaps are between: what managers think guests want and the standards they set; the standards set and what staff deliver; and what guests were promised (in advertising or by staff) and what is delivered. A guest who booked a villa package expecting a private chef that the package does not include shows a **promise-versus-delivery gap**: the problem is in how the offer was described, not in staff performance.

blocks.h: Moments of truth and the guest journey

blocks.p: A **moment of truth** is **any contact** in which a guest forms a view of the service: a phone call, a greeting, a clean glass, a bill. A **guest journey map** follows the guest from first search and booking, through arrival, stay and departure, to the follow-up, showing feelings and problems at each step. A **service blueprint** goes further: it shows the guest's actions, the staff actions the guest sees, the staff actions behind the scenes and the support systems (such as the booking system or laundry).

Every department is a customer of other departments. Housekeeping is the internal customer of the laundry; the front desk depends on housekeeping for room readiness. Poor service between departments soon reaches the guest. Quality managers therefore set standards for **internal service** too.

blocks.h: Why it matters: the cost of poor service

blocks.p: A guest lost through poor handling is lost for years. Example: a guest who stays three times a year and spends J$120,000 per stay is worth 3 × 120,000 = J$360,000 a year. Over four years the hotel could lose 360,000 × 4 = **J$1,440,000**, plus the reviews and recommendations that guest no longer gives. Winning back a guest costs far more than keeping one.

sections.title: Setting and rolling out service standards

blocks.p: A **service standard** states the level of service guests can expect. A good standard is **specific, measurable and achievable**. 'Greet each arriving guest within 30 seconds, with eye contact' is a standard. 'Give a warm welcome' is a hope: nobody can check it.

head: Weak wording
Better standard
rows: Answer the phone within three rings and give the department name and your own name
Each room cleaned and inspected to the checklist, and ready by 3:00 p.m.
Reply to every guest email within two hours between 7:00 a.m. and 9:00 p.m.
Use the guest's name at least twice in the first minute of a conversation

blocks.p: An **SOP** (standard operating procedure) is a written document that sets out, **step by step**, how a task such as check-in must be done. Standards say what result is expected; SOPs say how to achieve it. A **service charter** is a published statement telling guests the standards the hotel promises to meet.

flow: Find out what guests expect: surveys, reviews, complaint logs, talks with department heads
Map the guest journey and list the main contact points
Write a few clear, measurable standards for each point and SOPs for key tasks
Consult staff: they know what is practical and will own the standards
Train and coach with practice and role plays
Launch with a briefing and visible support from managers
Monitor, give feedback, recognise good performance
Review the standards regularly

ul: **Training** teaches the standard and why it matters. **Coaching** is on-the-job guidance with feedback.

If mystery guest reports show that operators often forget to use the caller's name, the best response is to **coach** the team, practise with role plays and re-check in a month. A written warning or removal from the job does not teach the skill.
A short **shift briefing** shares VIP arrivals, open guest issues, the day's focus and recognition. It is the daily tool for keeping standards alive.
Review the written standards **regularly**, and whenever guest needs or feedback change.

blocks.note: Standards belong to the whole hotel. Set them for internal service as well as guest contact points, and measure them. A standard no one measures is soon forgotten.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Method
Strengths
Weaknesses
rows: Cheap; numbers that can be tracked over time
Low response rates; problems found after the guest has left
Immediate; guests can write in the room
Few guests use them; those who do may be extreme
Show what future guests read; may reveal new issues
Not a balanced sample; mostly very happy or very unhappy guests; cannot be edited by the hotel
Tests standards against an agreed checklist; shows how staff act when no manager is watching
Records what guests tell staff; allows analysis
Only captures guests who speak up
Informal; relies on staff recording it

blocks.p: A mix works best. A small boutique hotel can combine a short post-stay survey, regular review monitoring and an occasional mystery guest visit. A **mystery guest** is a person who stays or visits as an ordinary guest and reports on the service against a checklist.

blocks.h: Why analyse online reviews as well as surveys?

blocks.p: Reviews show what **future guests** will read when deciding whether to book, and may reveal issues that surveys do not ask about. They are not more accurate than surveys, they do not replace training and the hotel cannot edit them.

Reply to reviews promptly, politely and in public where the review is public: thank the guest, accept fair points, say what has been done and invite them back. Never argue, blame the guest or ask friends to post good reviews. A hotel can set a target such as replying to 95% of reviews within 48 hours. If it replied to 57 of 60 reviews in time, it achieved 57 ÷ 60 × 100 = **95%**.

ul: To find where standards are not being met.
To spot trends and plan training.
To recognise staff whom guests praise by name.
It is **not** a sound reason to pick out guests to refuse bookings to later, or to find staff to blame.

blocks.p: A complaint is a gift: the guest has told you what is wrong. A **complaint log** records each one so that patterns can be found. Useful columns: date, guest and room, type of complaint, department, cause, action taken, outcome and whether the guest was satisfied. Do not record unnecessary personal data such as passport or card numbers.

To compare busy and quiet months fairly, use a **rate per 1,000 room nights**: complaints ÷ room nights sold × 1,000. Example: 27 complaints in a month when 5,400 room nights were sold: 27 ÷ 5,400 × 1,000 = **5 complaints per 1,000 room nights**. Check: 5 × 5.4 = 27.

blocks.h: Pareto chart: find the vital few

blocks.p: A **Pareto chart** ranks causes from largest to smallest, usually with a cumulative line, to show that a few causes account for most of the problem. Worked example: a hotel logged 160 complaints:
The top two types make up 65% of all complaints, so management should act on cleanliness and check-in first.

ul: **Five whys**: ask 'why?' again and again until the basic cause appears. Room keys keep failing. Why? The encoders lose their settings. Why? The batteries are old. Why? Nobody changes them. Why? There is no maintenance schedule. Root cause: no maintenance schedule.
**Fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram**: groups possible causes under main headings such as people, methods, equipment, materials, environment and management, for a group to discuss.
**Involve the teams** who do the work: housekeeping and front office together, when rooms are not ready.

blocks.p: Before choosing a fix, **find the root cause**. Telling the desk to apologise more, handing out vouchers to everyone or moving the standard check-in time do not solve why rooms are late.

If satisfaction scores fall every year between December and March, check first whether **staffing and supplies keep pace with peak occupancy**. Do not assume that guests in those months are simply harder to please.

**Service recovery** is the planned process of putting right a service failure and winning back the guest's goodwill. Mistakes will happen. How the hotel responds decides whether the guest leaves angry or loyal.

flow: Listen without interrupting; let the guest finish
Apologise sincerely for the experience; do not blame other people or departments
Confirm the facts and ask what the guest would like
Act: fix the problem now, within your authority
Offer fair amends where appropriate
Follow up to check the guest is satisfied
Record the complaint and its cause in the log
Use it to prevent a repeat

blocks.p: The staff member who hears the complaint **owns it** until it is solved or handed on properly. Apologising alone is not recovery: **put it right now, offer fair amends and follow up**. Telling the guest the kitchen was short-staffed, asking them to write a letter or promising that someone will be disciplined does not recover the situation.

The **service recovery paradox** is the finding that a guest whose problem was put right very well can end up more loyal than a guest who never had a problem. Never use this as an excuse to let failures happen.

**Empowerment** means giving front-line staff the authority to solve guest problems without first asking a manager. The benefit is that problems are solved fast at the first point of contact, anger is reduced and staff feel trusted. The risks: giving too much or too little, treating guests differently, fraud or pressure from demanding guests. Controls:

ul: A clear **limit** for each level, for example a front desk agent may give credits up to an amount set by management.
A **guideline** on what may be offered for which kind of problem, so offers are fair, consistent and in line with the problem.
**Log each credit** with its reason, and have a manager review the log.
Training and examples of good judgement.
No requirement that guests promise not to post a review, and no penalising staff for good-faith decisions within the limit.

blocks.p: A hotel allows a front desk agent to give a credit of up to J$12,000. A duty manager may approve up to J$40,000. A guest asks for J$35,000 after a missed wake-up call caused him to miss a meeting. The agent must call the duty manager, because the request is above her limit.

When a guest is still unhappy after the first offer, or threatens to post online or check out early, the case is **passed to a more senior manager** as the procedure says. The duty manager should not insist that the offer is final, call security to remove the guest, or make a much larger offer just to stop a post.

Deal first with **safety and health**. A guest stuck in a lift or an injured guest comes before an unhappy guest with a poor view or a late transfer. After first aid for an accident, record the incident, report it as required and check and make safe the area. Do not ask the guest to sign that the hotel is not at fault, and do not offer a stay in return for silence.

blocks.note: Guests remember how a problem was handled long after they forget the problem. A quick, sincere recovery by the first person who hears the complaint is worth more than a bigger offer later.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Measuring, monitoring and reporting service quality

head: Indicator
What it tells you
Example sum
rows: Whether guests will come back or recommend you

blocks.p: Average daily room rate and occupancy percentage are financial measures. They are useful, but they do not tell the manager directly whether guests are likely to return.
If satisfaction rose from 78% to 84%, it rose by **6 percentage points** (84 − 78). The relative increase is 6 ÷ 78 = about 7.7%. Do not mix the two.

To check a standard such as 'rooms ready by 3:00 p.m.', **track the time each room is released in the system, daily**, and report the percentage met. Asking staff each Friday, waiting for complaints or random monthly checks give weak or late information.
**Benchmarking** is comparing your guest scores and response times with those of the best similar hotels so you can learn and improve. It is not forecasting, up-selling or yield management.

After a change such as a new check-in procedure, compare **waiting times and guest scores before and after**. The opinion of the people who designed it, the number of new forms or the absence of letters to the general manager is not evidence.

A monthly guest service report should show **key results against targets, trends, causes and actions**: satisfaction score, review score, complaint rate with top complaint types, response times, recognitions and what is being done. It should not list the names and home details of guests, show only good comments or copy every comment card.
A resort spent J$30,000 putting right a family's spoiled holiday, and the family booked a return holiday worth J$450,000. The booking is worth 450,000 ÷ 30,000 = **15 times** the cost of recovery.

sections.title: Diverse guests, guest information and legal duties

ul: Keep the **same standards of respect and care** for every guest, and adapt how you deliver them.
Train staff on **likely expectations** of guests from other countries, but treat each guest as an individual person. Do not stereotype, and do not separate guests by nationality.

For guests with disabilities, ask about needs **before arrival**, confirm what the hotel can offer (an accessible room, step-free routes), brief staff and check that the room actually suits. Offer help without taking over, and speak to the guest, not the companion.
For older guests and families, think of seating, lighting, pace, children's menus and safety.
For guests with allergies or dietary needs, record them accurately, pass them to the kitchen and check at service.
Offer help in the guest's language where you can, with simple signs and translated menus.

blocks.p: A **guest history** record of returning guests' preferences lets you deliver personal service. The data protection law is about **collecting only what you need, keeping it secure and using it as agreed**. Do not share records with other firms for marketing, keep them for ever, or leave printouts at the front desk.

Consumer protection law has the general purpose of keeping advertising and prices honest. Describe rooms, facilities and prices **truthfully and clearly**, show extra charges before the guest books, and use your own photographs. Calling a room 'ocean view' because the sea can be seen from the roof misleads guests and creates complaints.
Hotels owe guests a duty of care. Keep pool areas, stairs and walkways safe, give first aid when needed, record and report incidents as required and learn from them.

Guests judge the whole experience, including contracted drivers, tour guides and restaurants. **Set standards in the contract, brief them and review their performance**. Telling guests that the driver is not employed by you, or stopping the service, does not solve the problem.

sections.title: Leading a service culture and planning for peak demand

blocks.p: A **service culture** is the shared belief among staff that caring for guests is everyone's job. Managers build it more by what they do than by what they say.

ul: **Model it**: be visible in guest areas, greet guests and staff, handle problems calmly.
**Recruit** for a positive attitude to guests, tested at interview, as well as for skills.
**Induct** new staff in the service values and standards.
**Equip** staff with training, tools, authority and clear standards.
**Recognise** staff who give great service, publicly and promptly.
**Communicate** at daily briefings; share guest compliments and lessons from complaints.
**Listen** to staff ideas; they know where service breaks down.
**Do not** leave service to human resources alone, or check uniforms closely and leave guest contact to chance.

blocks.p: In Jamaica the busiest tourist months run from about mid-December to April. When occupancy is above 90%, quality falls unless the hotel plans ahead:

flow: From September, review last season's complaints, scores and staffing
Forecast arrivals and occupancy week by week
Recruit and train seasonal staff early and pair them with experienced colleagues
Plan leave so key staff are present
Order linen, amenities and food in good time and agree supplier delivery dates
Add short briefings, extra checks and a surge plan for check-in and housekeeping
Review the results during and after the season and record lessons

blocks.p: A hotel's quality managers should keep the same standards at peak as in quiet months. They should not close in the busiest months, assume that guests are harder to please or cut checks to save time.

ul: I can name the five dimensions of service quality and find the weakest from a description.
I can explain expectations, gaps, moments of truth, guest journey maps and service blueprints.
I can write a measurable service standard and distinguish a standard, an SOP and a service charter.
I can plan a roll-out that includes consultation, training, coaching and briefings.
I can choose feedback methods and explain the strengths and weaknesses of each.
I can respond to online reviews.
I can calculate complaint rates per 1,000 room nights and percentage shares, and draw a Pareto conclusion.
I can use the five whys and a fishbone diagram to find a root cause.
I can carry out service recovery and set empowerment limits with controls.
I can decide priorities on a busy shift and handle an escalated complaint.
I can measure standards, benchmark, evaluate a change and report to owners.
I can serve diverse guests, protect guest data and report safety incidents.
I can build a service culture and plan for peak demand.

terms: Service quality
How well service meets or exceeds what guests expect.
SERVQUAL
Model of five dimensions: tangibles, reliability, responsiveness, assurance, empathy.
Moment of truth
Any contact in which a guest forms a view of the service.
Service standard
A specific, measurable statement of the service guests can expect.
SOP
Standard operating procedure: written, step-by-step instructions for a task.
Service charter
A published statement of the standards a hotel promises.
Mystery guest
A person who uses the hotel as an ordinary guest and reports against a checklist.
Pareto chart
A ranked chart that shows the vital few causes of most problems.
Fishbone diagram
A diagram (also called Ishikawa) that groups possible causes under headings.
Five whys
Asking 'why?' repeatedly to find the root cause.
Service recovery
Putting right a service failure and winning back the guest's goodwill.
Empowerment
Giving front-line staff authority to solve guest problems.
Benchmarking
Comparing results with the best similar organisations.
Internal customers
Colleagues and departments who receive service from others inside the hotel.
Guest history
The record of a returning guest's stays and preferences.
Service culture
The shared belief that caring for guests is everyone's job.

c1.title: A Runaway Bay hotel sets new standards
c1.text: A 45-room hotel in Runaway Bay has a new general manager, Ms Sophia Grant. Guests praise the setting but complain that service is uneven: some staff greet guests warmly, others do not. The hotel has no written standards. A mystery guest visit found that the telephone operators often forget to confirm requests. Ms Grant wants standards for the front desk, housekeeping and restaurant.

c2.title: A Falmouth hotel's complaint log
c2.text: A 90-room hotel in Falmouth logged 160 complaints last quarter: room cleanliness 64, slow check-in 40, noise 24, Wi-Fi 20 and food 12. The hotel sold 5,400 room nights in the quarter's busiest month, when it logged 27 of those complaints. The guest services manager, Mr Dwayne Ellis, wants to act on the data.

c3.title: A Kingston business hotel
c3.text: A Kingston business hotel allows front desk agents to give credits up to J$12,000 and duty managers up to J$40,000. A guest, Mr Aaron Mitchell, says that his wake-up call never came and he missed an early flight and an important meeting. He asks for J$35,000 and says he will write a harsh review if he is refused. The agent has apologised.

c4.title: A Montego Bay boutique hotel
c4.text: A 40-room boutique hotel in Montego Bay surveyed 300 guests last year and 270 rated their stay good or excellent. This year its online review score slipped and the manager, Ms Natalie Hall, wants to compare it with the best similar hotels. The hotel replied to 57 of 60 online reviews within 48 hours. After a spoiled stay, the hotel spent J$30,000 on recovery and the family booked a return stay worth J$450,000.

c5.title: A St Elizabeth eco-lodge
c5.text: A 24-room eco-lodge in St Elizabeth expects a group of French-speaking Canadian guests and a guest with a severe nut allergy. It uses a contracted driver for airport transfers, and guests have complained that he is often late. The lodge keeps guest preference records on a spreadsheet that is printed and left at the reception desk. Peak season is about to begin with occupancy above 90%.

questions.q: Ms Grant writes the draft standard 'Rooms ready by 3:00 p.m.' What must she add to make it work in practice?
o: A reminder that guests prefer rooms that are clean
A way to measure it and a named person to check it
A rule that supervisors may not enter occupied rooms
A bonus for the housekeeper who finishes first each day
questions.why: A standard works only when it can be measured and someone is responsible for checking it, for example by tracking the time each room is released. Reminders, restrictions and bonuses do not make it checkable.

questions.q: The mystery guest found that operators often forget to confirm requests. What is the best response?
o: Give every operator a written warning at once for the failure
Move all of the operators to other jobs inside the hotel
Remove the need to confirm requests from the written standard
Coach the team with role plays, then re-check
questions.why: The problem is a skill and habit gap, which coaching and practice address, followed by a re-check. Warnings or reassignments do not teach the skill, and removing the standard lowers quality.

questions.q: Which step should Ms Grant take first when writing the standards?
o: Find out what guests expect, using surveys and reviews
Copy the standards of the nearest big hotel to save time
Write standards for the housekeeping department only at first
Announce the standards at a staff meeting with no consultation
questions.why: Standards should be based on what guests expect and on what staff know is practical. Copying, covering one department or imposing standards without consultation reduces ownership and relevance.

questions.q: How should Ms Grant keep the standards alive after launch?
o: Hold one annual meeting where the standards are read out to staff
Display the standards on the wall of the manager's own office
Use short briefings, measure results and recognise good service
Ask staff to report on their own performance each Friday afternoon
questions.why: Daily briefings, measurement and recognition keep standards visible. An annual reading, a private display or self-reporting only does not keep them in daily practice.

questions.q: What share of the 160 complaints was about noise?
questions.why: 24 ÷ 160 × 100 = 15%. Wi-Fi, at 20 complaints, is 12.5%. A share is the part divided by the total.

questions.q: What was the complaint rate per 1,000 room nights in the busy month (27 complaints, 5,400 room nights)?
questions.why: 27 ÷ 5,400 × 1,000 = 5. Check: 5 × 5.4 = 27. A rate adjusts for how many room nights were sold.

questions.q: Room cleanliness is the largest complaint type. What should Mr Ellis do before choosing a fix?
o: Tell the housekeepers to work faster on all of the rooms
Add a notice in each room apologising for any untidiness found
Give every guest who complains a free breakfast the next day
Find the root cause with housekeeping and inspection staff
questions.why: Different causes need different fixes (training, supplies, staffing, inspection). Involve the teams and use the five whys. Pressure, notices or free breakfasts treat symptoms.

questions.q: Which tool would best let the team discuss possible causes under headings such as people, methods and equipment?
o: A Gantt chart for the project
A fishbone diagram
A balance sheet for the year
A weekly staff rota
questions.why: A fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram groups possible causes under headings for group analysis. The others do not serve this purpose.

questions.q: Mr Mitchell asks for J$35,000. Who should deal with it?
o: The agent, because she was the first one to hear the complaint
The guest's own company, which should pay for the missed meeting
The agent, who may give a smaller amount of her own choosing
The duty manager, as it is above the agent's limit
questions.why: Staff may act within their limit but must pass requests above it to the person with authority. The agent still owns the complaint until it is properly handed over.

questions.q: Which control should go with the empowerment scheme?
o: Allow credits only at weekends when the managers are away
Log each credit with its reason and review the log
Ask guests to promise that they will not post any reviews online
Make staff repay any credit that a manager thinks was too high
questions.why: Logging and review keeps empowerment fair and detects misuse. The others are unfair, counter-productive or punish good-faith decisions.

questions.q: Mr Mitchell says that he will post a harsh review. What is the best action for the duty manager?
o: Apologise, put it right within policy and follow up with the guest
Offer to cancel his bill on condition that he does not post a review
Tell him the hotel's decision is final and walk away
Call security to ask him to leave quietly
questions.why: Follow the recovery steps: apologise, fix, offer fair amends in line with the guideline and follow up. Buying silence, refusing or removing the guest escalates the problem.

questions.q: After the matter is settled, what should the hotel do with this complaint?
o: Delete the entry from the log, since it has been settled
Tell the staff that it was really the guest's own fault
Log the cause and fix the wake-up call process
Report it to the owners only if the guest posts the review
questions.why: Logging the cause and repairing the process prevents a repeat, which is the real purpose of recovery. Hiding or blaming prevents learning.

questions.q: What was the satisfaction rate among the 300 surveyed guests?
Which hotels should Ms Hall choose for her benchmarking?
o: The cheapest hotels in the town of Montego Bay
Any hotel with the highest room rates, whatever its type
The best-performing hotels of similar size and market
Her own hotel five years ago and no others
questions.why: Benchmarking compares performance with the best comparable organisations, so that the lessons can be applied. Cheap or very different hotels are not comparable, and looking only at the past is not benchmarking.

questions.q: What percentage of reviews did the hotel answer within 48 hours?
questions.why: 57 ÷ 60 × 100 = 95%. It is the share of all reviews answered in time.

questions.q: Many guests praise the Montego Bay staff for knowing the answers and being courteous. Which dimension of service quality is this?
o: Tangibles: the look of rooms and facilities
Reliability: doing what was promised on time
Responsiveness: speed in helping guests
Assurance: knowledge and courtesy
questions.why: Assurance is the staff's knowledge, courtesy and ability to inspire trust. Tangibles is physical appearance, reliability is delivering the promise accurately, and responsiveness is willingness and speed.

questions.q: What should the lodge do before arrival to look after the guest with the nut allergy?
o: Ask the guest to bring their own food to the lodge for the stay
Record the allergy, brief the kitchen and check at meals
Tell the kitchen to avoid nuts only on the day of the arrival
Rely on the guest to tell the waiter at every single meal
questions.why: Safety requires accurate records, kitchen briefing and checks at service. Shifting the burden to the guest or briefing once leaves risk.

questions.q: Which method would best show the lodge how often the contracted driver is late?
o: Record each pick-up time against the flight arrival time
Count the compliments written in the visitors' book each month
Ask the driver at the end of each month how he did
Wait for guests to post reviews and then count them all
questions.why: Records of actual times against the plan give a measurable, checkable answer for the contract review. Compliments, the driver's own view or reviews are partial and late.

questions.q: The preference records are printed and left at the reception desk. What is wrong with this?
o: Nothing is wrong, since all of the staff need to see the records
Printing guest records is not allowed under any rule or law
Records should be kept for ever to serve returning guests
Personal data must be kept secure and used as agreed
questions.why: The data protection law is about collecting only what is needed and keeping it secure. Leaving printouts in public view breaches this purpose.

questions.q: What is the best way to prepare for the peak season when occupancy is above 90%?
o: Wait to see how busy the first month is before adding any staff
Reduce the checks to save time during the busiest weeks of all
Review last season, forecast demand, and train staff early
Assume that the peak-season guests are simply harder to please
questions.why: Early planning of staff, training, supplies and checks protects quality at peak. Waiting, cutting checks or blaming guests lets service slip.
